name: Tijuana
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Tijuana: maquiladora and shelter partner diligence, IMMEX inventory losses and property title research.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Tijuana, scoped from Nashville: diligence on maquiladora suppliers, shelter operators and plant managers, fact-finding on inventory and customs-related losses under IMMEX, research on property titles in a city where registration gaps are common, and vetting of medical tourism providers.
intro: Tijuana is the largest city in Baja California, with 1,922,523 residents in INEGI's 2020 census, about 51 percent of the state's population. It sits on the border with San Diego and recorded more than 47 million transborder crossings in 2023, according to the municipal economic development secretariat. Manufacturing provides about a quarter of local employment: in the third quarter of 2023 the city had 617 manufacturing establishments in the IMMEX programme, roughly 64 percent of the state total, employing about 260,000 people. Medical devices are a leading specialisation, alongside electronics such as flat-screen televisions and aerospace components. Services, commerce, restaurants and hotels account for just over half of employment, and medical tourism draws patients from the United States.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Tijuana mainly because of its role in cross-border manufacturing. US and international manufacturers rely on contract manufacturers, shelter operators, logistics providers and local managers whose ownership, conduct and controls they cannot easily observe from across the border. IMMEX operations depend on accurate tracking of temporarily imported materials, so unexplained inventory losses or irregular dealings with vendors can create both financial and customs exposure. Real estate deals for plants, warehouses and homes meet a property registry in which many holdings have never been formally registered. Healthcare and insurance businesses that refer or reimburse patients treated in Tijuana want to know who owns the clinics involved.

matters.title: Maquiladora and shelter partner diligence
matters.text: Background research on contract manufacturers, shelter operators and their owners before a company moves production to Tijuana, covering corporate registrations, shareholders, litigation, tax and customs problems of record, and reputation, so the client understands who will hold its IMMEX status, employ its workforce and handle its materials.

matters.title: Inventory and customs-related losses
matters.text: Fact-finding for counsel when temporarily imported materials, finished goods or scrap cannot be reconciled, including research on the vendors, transport companies and employees involved, so the client can understand what happened and work with customs advisers on the IMMEX tracking and reporting consequences.

matters.title: Plant management and vendor misconduct
matters.text: Supporting internal investigations into suspected kickbacks, conflicts of interest or ghost suppliers in Tijuana plants by identifying links between managers, purchasing staff and the companies that supply labour, transport, maintenance, scrap and services, using registries and open sources and working through the client's counsel.

matters.title: Property title and ownership research
matters.text: Researching ownership and encumbrances of industrial and residential property before a lease, purchase or loan, recognising that property tax records do not establish legal title and that many Tijuana holdings rest on unregistered private contracts, so counsel can see where formal registration or court action is needed.

matters.title: Medical tourism provider vetting
matters.text: Background research on clinics, hospitals and physicians in Tijuana serving patients from the United States, including ownership, related companies, litigation, regulatory actions and adverse media, for insurers, employers, referral businesses and investors assessing who they are dealing with.

local_context.title: Public Property and Commerce Registry
local_context.text: Baja California's Registro Público de la Propiedad y del Comercio has a Tijuana delegation in the Zona Urbana Río. Its delegate said in 2024 that many residents still have not registered properties or businesses, often holding them under informal private contracts, and that ownership cannot change in the registry without a court ruling or notarised contract. Certificates of encumbrances and of ownership are key records for property diligence.

local_context.title: State courts in Tijuana
local_context.text: Baja California's Tribunal Superior de Justicia operates civil courts in Tijuana. In 2021 a registry module was opened inside the civil court building to deliver certified copies and certificates and, according to officials, to check whether court orders sent to the registry were genuine. That concern about forged orders is a reminder to verify registry entries and judgments at source. Federal courts also hear commercial matters.

local_context.title: IMMEX programme obligations
local_context.text: Most Tijuana export plants operate under IMMEX, which defers duties and VAT on temporarily imported materials. Participants must meet export thresholds, keep an inventory control system meeting Annex 24 requirements and report regularly to the tax authority (SAT) and the Secretaría de Economía. Many foreign companies start under a shelter provider's registration. These obligations shape what records exist and where losses become regulatory issues.

local_context.title: Cross-border economy
local_context.text: With San Diego across the border and Otay Mesa handling heavy commercial traffic, many Tijuana businesses have owners, managers, bank accounts and customers on both sides. Investigations frequently need to combine Mexican company and property records with US court, corporate and property records, using professionals licensed in each country for any field enquiries. Assets moved across the border, or companies with parallel US and Mexican entities, are common features of these matters.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Tijuana, TDSC begins by mapping which parts of the question sit in Mexico and which in the United States, since owners, assets and records often straddle the border. Research is conducted from Nashville using Mexican corporate and property registry information, published court records, US public records and Spanish- and English-language open sources. Where site visits, interviews or registry certificates are needed in Tijuana, TDSC coordinates with appropriately authorised local professionals and the client's Mexican counsel, and with customs advisers on IMMEX questions. Personal data is handled in line with Mexico's federal data protection law and collected only as the matter requires. TDSC does not use pretexting or seek access to restricted government records.

faqs.q: How do we vet a shelter operator or contract manufacturer in Tijuana?
faqs.a: We research the company's registration, shareholders and directors, related companies, litigation, and tax or customs problems of record, then check its claims about clients, capacity and experience against public information. Where a plant visit or reference interviews are justified, we coordinate with qualified local professionals and the client's Mexican counsel.

faqs.q: Can TDSC help investigate missing inventory at a Tijuana plant?
faqs.a: Yes. Working through the client's counsel, we help establish what records show about the materials, the vendors and carriers involved and the employees with access, and research links between them. Because IMMEX inventory controls and customs reporting may be affected, we coordinate with the client's customs advisers on any regulatory consequences.

faqs.q: Is a property tax receipt proof of ownership in Tijuana?
faqs.a: No. Tijuana's registry delegate has said that many people wrongly treat property tax records as proof of ownership. Legal title depends on registration with the Registro Público de la Propiedad y del Comercio, supported by a notarised deed or court ruling. We research registry records and encumbrance certificates obtained through proper channels and flag gaps for counsel.

faqs.q: Can you research a Tijuana clinic used by US patients?
faqs.a: Yes. We identify the clinic's owners, related entities and physicians, and review litigation, regulatory actions, professional information available from public sources and adverse media in Spanish and English. We report what can be verified and where Mexican records are limited, so clients can make referral, coverage or investment decisions on an informed basis.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have staff in Tijuana?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is headquartered in Nashville, Tennessee, and has no office or staff in Tijuana or elsewhere in Mexico. Most research is conducted remotely. Where work on the ground is needed, we coordinate with appropriately authorised local professionals and the client's counsel, and we decline requests involving restricted records or covert methods.

review_flags: Statement that federal courts also hear commercial matters reflects Mexico's concurrent jurisdiction in mercantile cases but is not tied to a fetched source; a PJBC bulletin titled 'Nuevo Tribunal Corporativo' appeared in search results but could not be opened, so any new Baja California corporate court is not mentioned.
Medical device employment figures from TECMA are dated (2010-2012) and are not used as current numbers; only the specialisation is stated.
IMMEX count differs between sources: SEDETI 617 establishments (Q3 2023) vs Tijuana EDC 595 active manufacturing companies; page uses SEDETI.
No arbitration centre in Tijuana and no Baja California-specific investigator licensing rule were verified within the search budget.
Time zone and DST alignment with California stated from general knowledge, not a fetched source.
